Pick an instrument you enjoy hearing and can access regularly. Consider cost, space, noise, and maintenance. If undecided, try a keyboard, guitar, or ukulele before buying; borrowing or renting is also an option.

[Step 02] **Set a small, measurable goal.**  
For example: “In four weeks, I will play one easy song from beginning to end at a steady, comfortable speed.” Schedule 15–20 minutes of practice on five days each week.

[Step 03] **Prepare your instrument and practice space.**  
Find a comfortable seat, good lighting, and a place where you can hear clearly. Get any necessary accessories, such as a tuner, pick, or instrument stand. Learn how to tune and care for your instrument using a beginner demonstration.

[Step 04] **Choose resources that do not require sheet music.**  
Find one beginner course with clear demonstrations and audio examples. Use guitar or ukulele tablature, chord diagrams, keyboard videos, or fingering charts as appropriate. Learn how your chosen resource shows which notes to play and how long to hold them.

[Step 05] **Learn the essential terminology.**  
Start with pitch, beat, rhythm, tempo, melody, and chord. Connect each word to something you can hear or play—for example, tap the beat while listening to a song.

[Step 06] **Learn comfortable posture and basic technique.**  
Follow a demonstration for holding or sitting at your instrument, positioning your hands, and producing a clear sound. For wind instruments, include breathing and mouth position. Keep movements relaxed; stop and adjust if playing causes pain.

[Step 07] **Find and play a few notes or chords.**  
Learn three to five notes for a melody instrument, or two easy chords for chord accompaniment. Use note names, string and fret numbers, or visual finger positions. Practice producing each sound clearly before connecting them.

[Step 08] **Practice keeping a steady beat.**  
Clap or tap along to a slow metronome, starting around 60 beats per minute. Then play one comfortable note or chord on each click. Once steady, try two evenly spaced sounds per click.

[Step 09] **Choose one genuinely easy song.**  
Look for a familiar melody using a few notes, or a song with two or three chords and a simple strumming pattern. Listen several times and hum or tap along before learning to play it.

[Step 10] **Learn the song in short sections.**  
Watch or listen to one small phrase, pause, and copy it. Practice only a few notes or one chord change at a time. Play slowly enough to control your movements, and repeat until you can perform the section correctly three times.

[Step 11] **Connect the sections and address difficult spots.**  
Join two sections, practicing the transition between them. If you repeatedly stumble, isolate the difficult movement and slow it down. Increase speed gradually—about five beats per minute—once it feels reliable.

[Step 12] **Use a repeatable practice routine.**  
For a 20-minute session, spend:

- 2 minutes setting up and checking tuning.
- 4 minutes on technique and rhythm.
- 10 minutes learning or improving your song.
- 4 minutes playing familiar material or experimenting.

[Step 13] **Develop your ear and experiment.**  
Try copying a short musical phrase by listening, humming it, and finding matching notes. Create a three-note melody or change the rhythm of something you know. Keep experiments short and enjoyable.

[Step 14] **Record yourself and get useful feedback.**  
Make a short recording each week. Listen for steady timing, clear sounds, and smooth transitions. Choose one thing to improve next; if possible, ask a teacher or experienced player to check your technique.

[Step 15] **Review progress and choose the next challenge.**  
Keep a simple log of practice time, sections learned, and comfortable playing speed. After you can play your first song steadily from beginning to end, choose another that adds just one new skill, such as a chord, note, or rhythm."}
